label: Person
name: Abd al-Hafid of Morocco
summary:
Abd al-Hafid ibn al-Hasan (1875-1937) was the Sultan of Morocco from 1908 to 1912 and a prominent member of the Alaouite Dynasty during a transformative period in North African history. Born in Fez, he rose to power in a context of imperial expansion and the struggle for sovereignty against external pressures. His younger brother, Abdelaziz of Morocco, preceded him, but Abd al-Hafid became increasingly critical of his sibling's diplomatic concessions to foreign powers, which he viewed as surrendering Moroccan autonomy.

In 1908, Abd al-Hafid orchestrated a coup that deposed Abdelaziz, positioning himself as a defender of traditional Moroccan sovereignty and Islamic values against encroaching European influence. However, his reign proved paradoxical: despite his initial anti-colonial stance, he found himself increasingly dependent upon French military and financial support to maintain domestic stability. This internal contradiction defined his brief rule, as he maneuvered between nationalist aspirations and the realities of European imperial power.

Ultimately, Abd al-Hafid signed the protectorate treaty with France in 1912, formally establishing French de facto control over Morocco while preserving the sultan's nominal authority. This treaty represented both a personal capitulation and a watershed moment in Moroccan history, marking the end of independent sultanate rule and the beginning of the colonial period. His reign exemplified the challenges faced by late 19th and early 20th-century monarchs navigating the pressures of industrialization, imperial expansion, and the erosion of traditional political authority. He died in 1937, having witnessed the full consolidation of the colonial system he had reluctantly accepted decades earlier.
